results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains several types of Kenyon cells. According to the VFB database, subclasses of [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") include [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") types, such as [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Kenyon cell of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, VFB records show that there are three main subtypes that project their axons to the gamma lobe, the alpha and beta lobes, and the alpha' and beta' lobes, which are referred to as alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells. These can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core, surface, posterior, anterior-posterior, middle, dorsal, and others. VFB holds 37 records of subclasses of Kenyon cell, as well as other relevant data, including [31468](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of Kenyon cell") images of Kenyon cell, [79](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,anatScRNAseqQuery "Run in VFB: scRNAseq data for Kenyon cell") scRNAseq data records, [91](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in Kenyon cell") records of transgene expression in Kenyon cell, [866](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for Kenyon cell") downstream connectivity classes, and [1006](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for Kenyon cell") upstream connectivity classes.

results.response: The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the mushroom body and lateral horn, according to the VFB database. It is also worth mentioning that another claim from VFB mentions "more than 125,000 neurons", but the context of this claim is unclear, and it does not specify the region or type of neurons.

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
The Drosophila central complex is a structure in the insect brain that plays a crucial role in navigation, locomotion, and spatial memory. According to the literature (e.g., Wolff et al., 2015; Heinze et al., 2013), the main components of the Drosophila central complex include the ellipsoid body, the protocerebral bridge, the noduli, and the fan-shaped body. 

VFB does not currently hold comprehensive data on the specific functions associated with each component of the Drosophila central complex. However, the connectome data indicates that these components are interconnected and form a network that is thought to be involved in the integration of sensory information and the control of motor behaviors. 

The literature suggests that the ellipsoid body is associated with spatial memory and visual navigation (e.g., Seelig et al., 2015), while the protocerebral bridge is thought to be involved in the processing of visual and polarized light information (e.g., Omoto et al., 2017). The fan-shaped body is associated with locomotion and motor control (e.g., Hanesch et al., 1989). 

VFB has annotated a number of neuroblast lineages and neuronal populations that contribute to the development and function of the central complex, but the exact relationships between these components and their associated functions are not fully characterized in the database. 

To further investigate the components and functions of the Drosophila central complex, users can query VFB for specific neuronal populations, neuroblast lineages, or synaptic connections, and explore the associated literature and datasets.

results.title: Circuit motif
results.question: Describe the dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs). Which DAN types connect to which MBON types?
results.response:
To describe the dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) and determine which types of adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons (DANs) connect to which types of MBONs, we can look at the available data in VFB. 

VFB holds data on the upstream connectivity classes for MBONs ([2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") records) and for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons ([1290](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") records), as well as downstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons ([316](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") records). These connectivity classes can provide insight into how different types of DANs connect to MBONs. 

Additionally, VFB has annotated subclasses of MBONs ([69](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of MBON") records) and subclasses of adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons ([21](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") records), which could help in understanding the specific types of DANs and MBONs involved in these connections. 

However, without specific data on the connectivity between individual subclasses of DANs and MBONs, we cannot determine the exact types of DANs that connect to which types of MBONs based on the information provided. 

The connectome data indicates potential connections between adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons and mushroom body output neurons, but the specific details of these connections would need to be derived from the upstream and downstream connectivity class data available in VFB. 

To further understand the dopaminergic input to MBONs, one could explore the available scRNAseq data for MBONs ([1](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,anatScRNAseqQuery "Run in VFB: scRNAseq data for MBON") record) and adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons ([22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,anatScRNAseqQuery "Run in VFB: scRNAseq data for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") records), as well as transgene expression data for both MBONs ([157](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in MBON") records) and adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons ([64](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") records), which might provide additional clues about the nature of these connections. 

In summary, while VFB holds extensive data on the connectivity and characteristics of MBONs and adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons, the exact connections between specific types of DANs and MBONs would require a detailed analysis of the available connectivity class data and other relevant records.

results.response: The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is known to be a type of neuron in the fly brain. According to the VFB database, LPLC2 is a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron whose cell body lies in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind. Its activity elicits a jump escape response, and it detects looming, or expansion, stimuli. VFB records show that LPLC2 is involved in detecting looming stimuli and triggering an escape response. However, VFB does not currently hold detailed information on the specific connections of LPLC2. results.title: Experimental planning
results.question: I want to study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. What neurons are involved, how are they connected, and what genetic tools can I use to access them?
results.response:
To study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, you can look into the available data on neurons involved in this behavior. VFB does not currently hold specific data on the neural circuit for CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. However, the literature suggests that certain neurons, such as those expressing the Gr21a and Gr63a receptors, are involved in CO2 detection (Suh et al., 2004; Jones et al., 2007). 

The connectome data indicates that these neurons are connected to other neurons in the antennal lobe and the mushroom body, which are brain regions known to be involved in olfactory processing (the connectome data from FlyEM). VFB holds records of neurons and their connections, but it does not currently hold data on the specific circuit for CO2 avoidance.

For accessing these neurons genetically, you can use tools such as the GAL4-UAS system, which allows for targeted expression of genes in specific neurons (Brand and Perrimon, 1993). VFB has annotated several GAL4 lines that can be used to target specific neurons, but it does not currently hold data on which lines specifically target the CO2-sensitive neurons.

To further investigate the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance, you can explore the available data on VFB and look into the literature for more information on the specific neurons and connections involved. You can also use tools such as FlyBase and Neuropil to find more information on the genetic tools available for accessing these neurons. 

Follow-up queries can be made to find more information on the specific neurons and connections involved in the CO2 avoidance circuit, and to explore the available genetic tools for accessing these neurons.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as noted by Thomas and Wyman (1984). VFB records show that there is one of these cells per hemisphere, with its large cell body located posterior to the lower protocerebrum, according to Koto et al. (1981). 

VFB holds [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") records of images of the giant fiber neuron, specifically DNp01, as well as [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01. The connectome data indicates that DNp01 has downstream connectivity classes ([361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records) and upstream connectivity classes ([435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records), which can be used to understand its connectivity. 

The Drosophila connectome reveals axo-axonic synapses on descending neurons, including the giant fiber neuron. VFB has annotated 10 genetic tool/expression pattern rows for the giant fiber neuron. 

For further information, you can explore the available images of DNp01, transgene expression in DNp01, downstream connectivity classes for DNp01, and upstream connectivity classes for DNp01, which are all available in VFB. Relevant publications include those by Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), and Namiki et al. (2018).
